events.location: Three fronts: Sinai, West Bank and Golan (marker at Jerusalem)
events.title: Six-Day War: Israel defeats Egypt, Jordan and Syria and occupies new territory
events.summary: On the morning of 5 June 1967, after a May crisis over Egypt's closure of the Straits of Tiran and its build-up in Sinai, Israel launched air strikes that destroyed most of the Egyptian air force and sent its army into Sinai and the Gaza Strip. Jordan opened fire the same day; Israeli forces took East Jerusalem and the West Bank by 7 June and reached the Suez Canal by 8 June. Israel attacked Syrian positions on the Golan Heights from 9 June, and the ceasefire demanded by UN Security Council resolutions 233 to 236 held on all fronts from the evening of 10 June. Israel's Ministry of Defense archive records 776 Israeli dead. No full official Arab toll exists; secondary estimates run to roughly 10,000-15,000 Egyptian, about 700 Jordanian and 1,000-2,500 Syrian soldiers killed. Israel now controlled Sinai, Gaza, the West Bank, East Jerusalem and the Golan Heights.

perspectives.framing: Presents the war as a pre-emptive act of self-defence against an imminent Arab attack, made unavoidable by the blockade of Eilat, the withdrawal of UN peacekeepers and Nasser's threats; the captured territories are described as security assets and, in the case of Jerusalem, as the reunification of Israel's capital.

Nasser's government initially described the 5 June strikes as aggression carried out with American and British help, a charge it later withdrew; Egypt frames the war as an Israeli attack whose results, the occupation of Arab land, had to be reversed.

Calls the war the Naksa, the 'setback', which placed the whole of Mandate Palestine under Israeli control and created a second wave of refugees, and regards the occupation that began in June 1967 as the central fact of Palestinian life since.

The Security Council confined itself to ceasefire demands during the fighting and then, in resolution 237, called on Israel to facilitate the return of inhabitants who had fled; UN usage refers to the territories taken in 1967 as occupied.

events.location: Allenby (King Hussein) Bridge, Jordan Valley, and the Golan Heights
events.title: 1967 displacement: hundreds of thousands flee the West Bank, Gaza and the Golan
events.summary: The June 1967 fighting set off the largest population movement since 1948. As Israeli forces took the West Bank, Gaza Strip and Golan Heights, hundreds of thousands of people crossed the Jordan River or fled toward Damascus, many of them 1948 refugees uprooted a second time. UNRWA's Commissioner-General reported that more than 300,000 people, including about 120,000 registered refugees, were rendered homeless or left their homes in the West Bank and Gaza; other estimates range from roughly 250,000 to 325,000. UNRWA reporting put Syrian movement from the Golan at about 80,000, others say up to 100,000, and an Israeli census in August 1967 found only about 6,400 Syrians remaining. Security Council resolution 237 of 14 June 1967 called on Israel to facilitate the return of those who had fled; Israel permitted only limited returns, and most of the displaced remained in Jordan and Syria. Palestinians call the episode the Naksa.

perspectives.framing: Describes the exodus as a second Nakba or the Naksa, attributing it to Israeli military pressure, the demolition of villages such as Imwas, Yalo and Beit Nuba near Latrun, and the refusal to allow return; the displaced are counted as refugees with a right of return.

Maintained that most people left of their own accord during the fighting or on Jordanian advice, offered a limited family-reunification scheme, and argued that the refugee question could only be settled within an overall peace agreement.

UNRWA registered the newly displaced as 'displaced persons' distinct from 1948 refugees and reported on their numbers; the Security Council and General Assembly called on Israel to facilitate their return.
Holds that the Golan's Arab population was expelled and its villages destroyed, and that the roughly 100,000 displaced and their descendants retain the right to return to the occupied Golan.

events.location: East Jerusalem (Old City and surrounding areas)
events.title: Israel extends its law and administration to East Jerusalem
events.summary: On 27 June 1967 the Knesset passed three laws enabling the government to extend Israeli law, jurisdiction and administration to any area of the former Mandate territory; on 28 June the government applied them to East Jerusalem and about 70 square kilometres of surrounding West Bank land held by Jordan since 1949, and dissolved the Arab municipal council. Israel described the step as municipal unification and denied that it amounted to annexation. The UN General Assembly, in resolution 2253 of 4 July 1967, adopted 99-0 with 20 abstentions including the United States, declared such measures invalid and called on Israel to rescind them; the Security Council reaffirmed this in resolution 252 of 21 May 1968. No state recognised the change. The enlarged municipality became the basis for Israeli neighbourhood construction beyond the 1949 line and remains one of the most contested questions in the conflict.

perspectives.framing: Framed the measures as the reunification of Jerusalem, Israel's eternal capital, guaranteeing free access to holy places of all faiths; it insisted at the time that the laws were administrative rather than an annexation, a position later formalised in the 1980 Basic Law: Jerusalem.

Denounced the annexation of a city it had administered since 1948, retained its claim to the West Bank until 1988 and continued to assert custodianship of the Muslim holy places, including the Haram al-Sharif / Temple Mount.

The General Assembly and Security Council held that measures changing the status of Jerusalem are invalid, that acquisition of territory by military conquest is inadmissible, and that East Jerusalem is occupied territory.

Regards East Jerusalem as the capital of a future Palestinian state and describes the expansion of the municipal boundary, land expropriations and residency rules as steps in the city's annexation and Judaisation.

events.title: Arab summit at Khartoum adopts the 'three noes' resolution
events.summary: Arab heads of state met in Khartoum from 29 August to 1 September 1967 to coordinate their response to the June defeat. The summit resolution adopted on 1 September pledged to unite Arab political and diplomatic efforts to 'eliminate the effects of the aggression' and secure Israeli withdrawal from occupied Arab land 'within the framework of the main principles to which the Arab states adhere, namely: no peace with Israel, no recognition of Israel, no negotiations with it, and adherence to the rights of the Palestinian people in their country'. It also arranged Saudi, Kuwaiti and Libyan subsidies for Egypt and Jordan and ended the wartime oil embargo. Syria boycotted the meeting and the PLO chairman walked out. American officials read the outcome as a modest step toward realism by Nasser and King Hussein, while Israel cited the 'three noes' as proof that no Arab partner for peace existed.

perspectives.framing: Presented the resolution as a unified rejection of negotiating under occupation and a commitment to recover the occupied territories by political means, while restoring Arab solidarity and financial support for the front-line states.
Cited the 'three noes' for decades as evidence of Arab rejectionism that justified holding the territories pending direct negotiations and a peace treaty.
Officials privately judged that Khartoum marked 'a first short step toward realism', noting the endorsement of political rather than military means and the moderates' influence over the outcome.

Many read the resolution as ambiguous, arguing that Nasser and Hussein used it to legitimise a diplomatic path leading to their acceptance of resolution 242, whereas others see it as confirming Arab refusal of peace.

events.location: Kfar Etzion, between Bethlehem and Hebron, Israeli-occupied West Bank
events.title: Kfar Etzion re-established: first Israeli settlement in the occupied West Bank
events.summary: On 27 September 1967 a group of young Israelis, many of them children of kibbutz members killed there in May 1948, re-established Kfar Etzion between Bethlehem and Hebron in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, the first civilian Israeli settlement in territory captured in June. Levi Eshkol's government had announced the plan days earlier together with outposts on the Golan and at the northern Dead Sea, describing the sites to the United States as Nahal 'strongpoints' rather than settlements. The move followed the unofficial Allon Plan, drafted by minister Yigal Allon in July 1967, which proposed a line of Israeli settlements along the Jordan Valley and around Jerusalem while returning populated highland areas to Jordan. US diplomats reported by early 1968 that the outposts were becoming permanent civilian kibbutzim. Kfar Etzion began a settlement enterprise that by the 2020s encompassed several hundred thousand Israelis in the West Bank.

perspectives.framing: Described the early sites as security strongpoints in Judea and Samaria and the Golan, and Kfar Etzion specifically as the return of a community destroyed in 1948; later governments refer to settlements as communities and dispute that the Fourth Geneva Convention applies to the West Bank.

Regards settlements as colonies built on confiscated Palestinian land that entrench the occupation and pre-empt a Palestinian state, and points to Kfar Etzion as the start of a deliberate policy rather than a spontaneous return.

Holds that settlements in territory occupied in 1967 have no legal validity and breach the Fourth Geneva Convention, a position later set out in Security Council resolutions 446 (1979) and 2334 (2016).
In 1967-68 Washington privately asked Israel to avoid steps that would appear to prejudge a settlement, and reported that the 'strongpoints' were taking on a permanent civilian character.

events.title: UN Security Council adopts Resolution 242 on 'land for peace'
events.summary: On 22 November 1967 the UN Security Council unanimously adopted the British-drafted resolution 242, the framework for later Arab-Israeli negotiations. Emphasising 'the inadmissibility of the acquisition of territory by war', it affirmed that a just and lasting peace should include 'withdrawal of Israeli armed forces from territories occupied in the recent conflict' and 'termination of all claims or states of belligerency', with respect for every state's right 'to live in peace within secure and recognized boundaries'. It also called for freedom of navigation and 'a just settlement of the refugee problem', and provided for a special representative, Gunnar Jarring. Because the English text has no definite article before 'territories', Israel argued that withdrawal need not be total, while Arab states, citing the French text, insisted on full withdrawal. Egypt and Jordan accepted it; Syria rejected it until 1973, and the PLO rejected it as treating Palestinians only as refugees.

perspectives.framing: Reads the resolution as requiring withdrawal only to 'secure and recognized boundaries' negotiated directly with Arab states, not to the 1949 lines, and as linking any withdrawal to peace, an end of belligerency and recognition.

Accepted the resolution as requiring complete Israeli withdrawal from all territories occupied in June 1967 before or as part of any settlement, citing the preamble on the inadmissibility of acquiring territory by war and the French text.
Rejected the resolution for two decades because it referred to Palestinians only as a 'refugee problem' and did not recognise their national rights; the PLO accepted it, with 338, in 1988.

As the drafter, Lord Caradon described the wording as deliberately balanced and denied that the missing article was accidental, insisting that the emphasis lay on the inadmissibility of acquiring territory by war combined with secure boundaries.

events.title: Battle of Karameh: Israeli raid into Jordan meets Fatah and Jordanian resistance
events.summary: Before dawn on 21 March 1968 Israeli forces crossed the Damiya and Allenby bridges into Jordan with armour and air support to attack Fatah bases at Karameh, a Jordan Valley town used for raids into the occupied West Bank, and at Safi south of the Dead Sea. President Johnson's appeal to Eshkol against a reprisal arrived three hours after the operation began. Fatah fighters, joined by Jordanian army artillery and armour, resisted through the day before the Israelis withdrew, having demolished much of the town. Casualty figures are disputed: Israeli figures cite 28 to 33 Israeli soldiers killed, Jordan reported several dozen soldiers dead and Palestinian fighters killed are put at roughly 100 to 200. On 24 March the UN Security Council condemned the 'large-scale and carefully planned' Israeli action in resolution 248. Fatah presented the battle as a victory, and thousands of recruits joined Fatah.

perspectives.framing: Described the operation as a necessary reaction to terrorism after a mine attack on a school bus, aimed at destroying guerrilla bases, and reported that it had localised the fighting and spared civilians.

Fatah calls Karameh (Arabic for 'dignity') the moment the Palestinian resistance stood its ground against the Israeli army, a founding myth that made Yasser Arafat the movement's leader and brought a surge of volunteers.

Credits the Jordanian army's artillery and armour with inflicting the losses that forced the Israeli withdrawal, while the episode also deepened its unease at the fedayeen's growing autonomy on Jordanian soil.
The Security Council deplored the loss of life, condemned the Israeli military action as a violation of the ceasefire and warned that further such acts would lead it to consider more effective steps.

events.title: Israeli commandos destroy 13 airliners at Beirut airport after Athens attack
events.summary: On 26 December 1968 two members of the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine attacked an El Al airliner at Athens airport, killing one Israeli passenger. Holding Lebanon responsible for a group that operated from its territory, Israel retaliated on the night of 28 December: about 45 commandos landed by helicopter at Beirut International Airport and destroyed thirteen Lebanese-owned civilian aircraft in a twenty-minute operation without loss of life. Lebanon, which had stayed out of the 1967 war, protested to the UN Security Council, which on 31 December unanimously adopted resolution 262 condemning Israel for a 'premeditated' attack on a civil airport and holding that Lebanon was entitled to appropriate redress. France, whose helicopters and aircraft were used, tightened its arms embargo on Israel. The raid opened a cycle of Palestinian operations from Lebanon and Israeli reprisals that would dominate the Israel-Lebanon frontier.

perspectives.framing: Justified the raid as a proportionate response to a terrorist attack planned in Beirut, deliberately aimed at property rather than lives, and as a warning to Arab states hosting armed Palestinian groups.

Condemned an unprovoked attack on a neutral country's civil aviation and sought international redress, while facing growing domestic pressure over the Palestinian armed presence that led to the 1969 Cairo Agreement.
The Security Council condemned Israel for a premeditated, large-scale and carefully planned military action against a civil airport and warned of further steps in the event of repetition.
The PFLP claimed the Athens attack as a legitimate operation against Israel's national airline and presented the Beirut raid as proof of Israeli aggression against Arab states.

events.title: War of Attrition along the Suez Canal ends in a US-brokered standstill ceasefire
events.summary: After months of intermittent clashes along the Suez Canal, Egypt's president Gamal Abdel Nasser declared early in 1969 that the 1967 ceasefire was void and opened sustained artillery, commando and air attacks intended to make Israel's hold on the east bank of the Canal too costly; the campaign is usually dated from 8 March 1969. Israel replied with air strikes along the Canal and, from January 1970, deep-penetration bombing near Cairo, which led the Soviet Union to send air-defence crews and pilots to Egypt; Israeli and Soviet-flown aircraft fought directly in July 1970. A United States proposal by Secretary of State William Rogers produced a 90-day standstill ceasefire effective at 22:00 GMT on 7 August 1970, later extended. Estimates of the dead vary widely in the secondary literature, from several hundred to more than a thousand Israelis and from about 3,000 to 10,000 Egyptians.

perspectives.framing: Framed the campaign as a war to liberate occupied Sinai by imposing unacceptable losses on Israel, and treated the 1970 ceasefire as a pause that allowed missile batteries to be moved to the Canal in preparation for a crossing.

Described the fighting as Egyptian violations of the ceasefire that justified deep-penetration raids to punish Nasser, and complained that Egypt breached the August 1970 standstill by moving surface-to-air missiles forward.
Saw the war as a dangerous superpower flashpoint after Soviet forces arrived in Egypt, and promoted the Rogers initiative to secure a ceasefire and revive the Jarring mission under resolution 242.

Debate whether the war was an Egyptian failure or a strategic success, noting that Soviet involvement, the missile wall built during the ceasefire and Israeli overconfidence shaped the surprise of October 1973.

events.title: Black September: Jordan's army fights Palestinian armed groups
events.summary: Tension between King Hussein and the Palestinian armed organisations based in Jordan peaked after the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine hijacked four airliners on 6 September 1970 and blew up three of them at Dawson's Field near Zarqa. On 16 September the King declared martial law and installed a military cabinet; the next day the army attacked fedayeen positions in Amman and elsewhere. Syrian armoured brigades crossed into northern Jordan on 20 September but withdrew after Jordanian air strikes and Israeli and American threats. On 27 September Hussein and Yasser Arafat signed a ceasefire in Cairo brokered by Nasser, who died the next day. The CIA recorded Arafat claiming more than 7,000 casualties in the Amman camps; later secondary estimates range from about 3,000 to 5,000 dead. Fighting resumed in 1971 until the PLO was expelled to Lebanon; the Black September Organisation took its name from these events.

perspectives.framing: Presents the campaign as the restoration of state authority against armed groups that had created a state within a state, hijacked aircraft on Jordanian soil and threatened the monarchy, and stresses the Syrian invasion as a foreign attack repelled by the army.

Calls the events Black September, a massacre of Palestinian fighters and refugees by a regime acting in concert with Israel and the United States; the expulsion to Lebanon is remembered as a betrayal by an Arab government.
Treated the crisis as a Cold War test, moving the Sixth Fleet and coordinating with Israel to deter Syria, and credited Hussein's victory with averting a wider war.

Justified its incursion as support for the Palestinian resistance under the banner of the Palestine Liberation Army and withdrew amid the refusal of its air force commander, Hafez al-Assad, to commit aircraft.

events.title: Munich Olympics attack: eleven Israeli team members killed
events.summary: Early on 5 September 1972 eight members of the Palestinian Black September Organisation entered the Olympic Village in Munich, West Germany, and broke into the Israeli team's quarters, killing wrestling coach Moshe Weinberg and weightlifter Yossef Romano and seizing nine other athletes and officials. They demanded the release of more than 200 prisoners held in Israel; Israel refused, and after a day of negotiation the West German authorities flew the attackers and hostages by helicopter to Fürstenfeldbruck air base, where a rescue attempt collapsed into a gunfight. All nine hostages were killed, along with a West German police officer and five of the attackers; the three surviving attackers were captured and released in October after a Lufthansa hijacking. The Games resumed after a one-day pause. Israel bombed Palestinian bases in Syria and Lebanon within days and began a covert campaign against those it held responsible for the attack.

perspectives.framing: Describes the attack as a terrorist massacre of unarmed athletes, criticises the German rescue operation and the later release of the surviving attackers, and treated the assassination of Black September figures as legitimate counter-terrorism.

Black September, linked to Fatah, presented the operation as an act of the Palestinian resistance intended to free prisoners and force the world to notice the Palestinian cause; the PLO leadership publicly distanced itself from the group by 1974.

Acknowledged the failure of an improvised police operation and the lack of specialist forces, created the GSG 9 counter-terrorism unit, and in 2022 formally apologised and agreed compensation with the victims' families.
Under Avery Brundage the IOC insisted that 'the Games must go on', resuming competition after a memorial service; it has since honoured the victims at later Games.

events.title: October War (Yom Kippur / Ramadan War): Egypt and Syria attack Israeli forces
events.summary: At 2 p.m. on 6 October 1973, Yom Kippur and during Ramadan, Egypt and Syria launched a coordinated surprise attack on Israeli forces in occupied Sinai and the Golan Heights. Egyptian troops crossed the Suez Canal and overran the Bar-Lev Line, while Syrian armour broke into the Golan. After heavy initial losses Israel drove Syrian forces back beyond the 1967 line toward Damascus and from 15 October crossed the Canal, encircling Egypt's Third Army; the superpowers airlifted arms to the combatants. The war ended through UN Security Council resolutions 338 (22 October), 339 and 340 (25 October), which created a new UN Emergency Force. Israel's State Archives record about 2,656 Israeli soldiers killed; Golda Meir gave Henry Kissinger a figure of 1,500 to 2,000 dead during the fighting. Egypt and Syria issued no agreed totals; secondary estimates run to roughly 8,000 to 18,500 Arab soldiers killed.

perspectives.framing: Celebrates 6 October as the day the army crossed the Canal and 'restored Arab dignity', treating the war as a victory that broke the post-1967 deadlock and led to the recovery of Sinai; Egyptian accounts play down the later Israeli crossing.

Calls it the Yom Kippur War, a surprise attack that Israel repelled at great cost; the Agranat Commission blamed intelligence and command failures, and the shock reshaped Israeli politics and led to the 1977 change of government.
Presents the October War of Liberation as a coordinated effort to recover the Golan that was undercut when Egypt accepted a ceasefire, and emphasises the return of Quneitra in 1974 as its outcome.

Framed its airlift and diplomacy as preventing an Israeli defeat while avoiding a humiliation of Egypt, and used the outcome to displace Soviet influence in Cairo and launch step-by-step negotiations.

events.title: Arab oil producers cut output and embargo the United States
events.summary: On 17 October 1973 Arab oil ministers meeting in Kuwait announced that their states would cut production by 5 per cent at once and by a further 5 per cent each month until Israel withdrew from the territories occupied in 1967 and Palestinian rights were restored. After President Nixon asked Congress on 19 October for 2.2 billion dollars in emergency military aid for Israel, Libya and then, on 20 October, Saudi Arabia announced a complete halt of oil exports to the United States, later extended to the Netherlands and other states. The posted price of Gulf crude roughly quadrupled between October and January. Arab producers lifted the embargo on the United States at a meeting in Vienna on 18 March 1974, after the Egypt-Israel disengagement agreement and American mediation with Syria. The measures caused shortages and recession in importing countries and demonstrated Arab producers' political leverage.

perspectives.framing: Producers presented the cuts and embargo as a legitimate use of Arab resources to support Egypt and Syria and to press the United States and Europe to compel Israeli withdrawal under resolution 242.

Condemned the embargo as blackmail and a threat to the world economy, launched 'Project Independence', and used Kissinger's shuttle diplomacy partly to secure its lifting; the Office of the Historian records the episode as a turning point in US energy policy.
Saw the embargo as evidence that Arab states would use economic warfare against Israel's allies, and worried that Western dependence on Arab oil would erode support for Israel.
Stress that the price rise owed as much to OPEC's unilateral posted-price decisions as to the embargo itself, and debate how far the embargo changed Western policy toward the conflict.

events.title: UN Security Council Resolution 338 calls for a ceasefire and negotiations
events.summary: At 12:50 a.m. New York time on 22 October 1973 the UN Security Council adopted resolution 338, a US-Soviet draft negotiated in Moscow by Kissinger and Brezhnev, by 14 votes to none with China not participating. It called on all parties 'to cease all firing and terminate all military activity' within twelve hours in the positions they occupied, called for implementation of resolution 242 'in all of its parts', and decided that negotiations 'between the parties concerned under appropriate auspices' should begin immediately and concurrently with the ceasefire. Egypt and Israel ordered a ceasefire for 18:52 local time, but fighting continued as Israeli forces completed the encirclement of Egypt's Third Army; the Council reaffirmed the ceasefire in resolution 339 on 23 October and created UNEF II in resolution 340 on 25 October. With 242, resolution 338 became the agreed basis for later Arab-Israeli negotiations.

perspectives.framing: Kissinger presented the resolution as a superpower agreement that ended the war on terms preserving Israel's battlefield position while committing the parties, for the first time, to direct negotiations under American auspices.

Accepted the ceasefire to save the Third Army and read the call for negotiations 'under appropriate auspices' as leading to full Israeli withdrawal under 242; Egypt accused Israel of violating the ceasefire by advancing after 22 October.

Accepted the resolution under American pressure, valued its call for negotiations between the parties, and disputed Egyptian claims about the 22 October lines when the Council demanded a return to them.

Accepted 338 only on 23 October and with the understanding that it required Israeli withdrawal from all territories occupied in 1967 and respect for Palestinian rights; this marked Syria's first acceptance of resolution 242.

events.title: Egypt and Israel sign the Sinai I disengagement agreement at Kilometre 101
events.summary: On 18 January 1974 the chiefs of staff of Egypt and Israel signed the first disengagement of forces agreement, known as Sinai I, at Kilometre 101 on the Cairo-Suez road, witnessed by UNEF commander General Ensio Siilasvuo. It followed a week of shuttle diplomacy by Henry Kissinger between Aswan and Jerusalem, after the Kilometre 101 military talks and the Geneva Conference of December 1973. Israel agreed to withdraw from the west bank of the Suez Canal and from a strip east of it, Egypt kept a limited force on the east bank, and a UN buffer zone separated the sides, with restricted-armament zones beyond it monitored by UNEF and American aerial reconnaissance. Implementation was completed by early March 1974, allowing Egypt to reopen the Canal in 1975. The agreement ended the siege of Egypt's Third Army and was the first Egypt-Israel accord since the 1949 armistice.

perspectives.framing: President Sadat presented the agreement as the first fruit of the October crossing, restoring Egyptian sovereignty over the east bank of the Canal and opening a diplomatic path, backed by the United States, toward full recovery of Sinai.

Prime Minister Meir's government accepted withdrawal from the Canal in return for the release of the Third Army pressure, prisoner exchanges, limitations on Egyptian forces and an American commitment to Israel's security, describing it as separation of forces rather than a political settlement.
Kissinger treated Sinai I as proof that step-by-step diplomacy under American auspices could produce results where the Geneva framework could not, and as leverage for lifting the Arab oil embargo.
UNEF II supervised the disengagement, manned the buffer zone and inspected the limited-forces zones, reporting to the Security Council under resolution 340.

events.title: Israel and Syria sign a disengagement agreement; UNDOF created
events.summary: After 32 days of Kissinger's shuttle diplomacy between Damascus and Jerusalem, and months of artillery duels on the Golan front, Israel and Syria signed an Agreement on Disengagement in the Egyptian-Israeli military working group of the Geneva Conference on 31 May 1974. Israel undertook to withdraw from the salient it had captured in October 1973 and from the town of Quneitra and a narrow strip along the 1967 ceasefire line, which returned to Syrian civil administration; an area of separation patrolled by a new UN Disengagement Observer Force (UNDOF), created the same day by Security Council resolution 350, and equal zones of limited forces and armaments were established on either side. Prisoners of war were exchanged in June. The agreement ended the fighting of the October War on the Syrian front, and UNDOF's mandate has been renewed at six-month intervals ever since.

perspectives.framing: President Assad presented the agreement as recovering Quneitra and the 1973 losses without recognising Israel, insisting it was a military disengagement and only a first step toward full Israeli withdrawal from the Golan; Syria accused Israel of razing Quneitra before handing it over.

Valued the agreement for ending the war of attrition on the Golan, securing the return of Israeli prisoners and obtaining a Syrian commitment against guerrilla attacks from its territory, while retaining the Golan plateau captured in 1967.
Kissinger regarded the accord as his most difficult negotiation, extending step-by-step diplomacy to Israel's most hostile neighbour and enabling the Arab oil embargo to remain lifted.
The Security Council welcomed the agreement as implementing resolution 338 and created UNDOF to supervise the area of separation, an arrangement it has renewed every six months since 1974.

boundaryChanges.description: Israeli forces complete the capture of East Jerusalem (Old City) and the West Bank from Jordan; the territory passes from Jordanian administration to Israeli military occupation, with the 1949 armistice line becoming the Green Line.

Israeli forces reach the Suez Canal and the Red Sea, completing the occupation of the Sinai Peninsula and the Gaza Strip, previously under Egyptian control and administration; the Canal becomes the de facto ceasefire line and is closed to shipping.

Ceasefire on the Syrian front at 16:30 GMT leaves Israel in occupation of the Golan Heights up to a line east of Quneitra; Security Council resolution 236 calls for a return to the ceasefire positions of that hour.

Israel applies its law, jurisdiction and administration to East Jerusalem and about 70 square kilometres of surrounding West Bank land, enlarging the Jerusalem municipality; the annexation is not recognised internationally (UNGA 2253, UNSC 252).

October War ceasefire lines: Egyptian forces hold two bridgeheads on the east bank of the Suez Canal while Israeli forces hold a salient west of the Canal encircling the Egyptian Third Army; on the Golan, Israeli forces hold a salient beyond the 1967 line toward Sa'sa'. UNEF II is created to supervise the Egyptian front.

Sinai I: Israel withdraws from the west bank of the Suez Canal and from a strip east of it; Egypt holds a limited-forces zone along the east bank, a UNEF buffer zone separates the sides and limited-armament zones extend beyond it (implemented by early March 1974).

Israel-Syria disengagement: Israel withdraws from the 1973 salient and from Quneitra and a strip along the 1967 line; a UNDOF-patrolled area of separation and two limited-forces zones are established on the Golan (implemented by late June 1974).

uncertainties: Research-environment limitation (critical): the WebSearch budget was exhausted (200/200) before this unit began, and the organisation's egress proxy returned CONNECT 403 for every publisher host tried by both WebFetch and curl (un.org, unrwa.org, peacemaker.un.org, undocs.org, digitallibrary.un.org, britannica.com, history.state.gov, avalon.law.yale.edu, gov.il, knesset.gov.il, btselem.org, aljazeera.com, bbc.co.uk, theguardian.com, nytimes.com, apnews.com, reuters.com, icrc.org, hrw.org, olympics.com, jstor.org, refworld.org and others). Only GitHub (api.github.com, raw.githubusercontent.com) was reachable. Primary-source content was therefore read from GitHub mirrors of the same publications: the full TEI XML of FRUS volumes 1964-68 XIX and XX and 1969-76 XXIII, XXIV, XXV, XXVI and XXXVI (HistoryAtState/frus), and the full texts of UN Security Council resolutions 233-237, 242, 248, 252, 262, 338-340 and 350 (felixhaass/pvs_securitycouncil dataset, which reproduces the UN/Refworld texts including their Refworld URLs). FRUS document URLs follow the canonical history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/<volume>/<document> scheme derived from the xml:id of each document read. Every other cited URL is either (a) a URL taken from sibling research files in this repository that came from live search listings earlier in the session, or (b) an exact URL string found verbatim in public citation corpora via GitHub code search (for example the UN Peacemaker, Security Council Report, UNISPAL, UNRWA, B'Tselem, Al Jazeera, IOC, Federal Reserve History, Israel Ministry of Defense Archives, Israel State Archives, Akevot and Avalon pages). No cited page was opened directly. A link check (npm run validate -- --links) and a fact re-check from an unrestricted network are required; verified:true was set only where the date and core facts were confirmed in at least two independently published texts actually read (FRUS documents plus UN resolution texts or the scraped text of Al Jazeera's PLO chronology).

Verification status: verified:false was set for six events whose core facts were confirmed only in FRUS documents (one publisher) or whose key figures were taken from a compiled dataset rather than the primary report: the 1967 displacement (UNRWA figures via a dataset citing the Commissioner-General's report), the Khartoum Resolution, the Kfar Etzion / Allon Plan entry, the War of Attrition, the Arab oil embargo and the Sinai I agreement. Their dates and narrative are consistent with the standard literature and with the FRUS record read here; they should be flipped to true once a second source is opened.

Six-Day War casualties: the Israeli figure of 776 comes from the Israel Ministry of Defense Archives page as cited in a compiled dataset (another ministry page gives 736 and secondary tables up to 983). Arab figures are secondary-literature ranges; a contemporaneous diplomatic report recorded in FRUS (1964-68 XIX, Document 394) quotes an Egyptian source giving 20,000 Egyptian dead against an earlier figure of 5,000.

1967 displacement: UNRWA's figure of 'more than 300,000, including about 120,000 registered refugees' and the Syrian figure of about 80,000 were read in a compiled dataset that cites the UNRWA Commissioner-General's report (UNISPAL document auto-insert-198325) and a second UNISPAL document (auto-insert-177212) whose exact title could not be confirmed; the second document's title in the sources list is descriptive. The 6,400 figure for Syrians remaining comes from the Akevot Institute article as cited. Historians' totals for Palestinians range from about 250,000 to 325,000.

East Jerusalem: FRUS records the three Knesset laws of 27 June 1967 and the government's administrative action of 28 June; the area figure of about 70 square kilometres is the commonly cited figure (UN and B'Tselem) and was not read in a primary source here. The UNGA vote (99-0-20) is from FRUS Document 344.

Kfar Etzion: FRUS confirms Eshkol's announcement of settlements at Baniyas, Etzion and Beit Haarava around 24-25 September 1967 and Israel's description of them as Nahal 'strongpoints'; the exact establishment date of 27 September 1967 is the standard date in the literature (Peace Now's settlement database lists Kfar Etzion's founding year as 1967) and was not read in a primary source.

Karameh casualties: none of the figures (Israeli 28-33 killed; Jordanian about 40-84; Palestinian about 100-200) was read in a primary source; FRUS Document 119 confirms the date, the crossing points and the Israeli justification, and Security Council resolution 248 confirms the international response.

War of Attrition: the start date of 8 March 1969 is the conventional date; the FRUS documents read confirm Israeli assessments of Egypt's 'war of attrition' in 1969 and the standstill ceasefire effective 2200 GMT on 7 August 1970 (initially 90 days, to 5 November). The Britannica URL cited is the older 'EBchecked' form found verbatim in a citation corpus and is expected to redirect. Casualty totals are contested and are given only as ranges.

Black September: the '7,000 casualties' figure is Arafat's claim as relayed by CIA Director Helms during the fighting (FRUS 1969-76 XXIV, Document 313) and covers killed and wounded; the 3,000-5,000 death estimate is the secondary-literature range and was not read in a primary source. The event is dated from the martial-law declaration of 16 September to the Cairo ceasefire of 27 September 1970, with the 6 September hijackings described as the trigger.

Munich: the White House memorandum of 6 September 1972 (FRUS) says two athletes were killed in the village and nine at Furstenfeldbruck, with 'four of their captors' dying; standard later accounts give five attackers and one West German policeman killed. Both are recorded.

October War: the figure of about 2,656 Israeli soldiers killed is attributed to the Israel State Archives' 50th-anniversary publication as cited in a compiled dataset (other Israeli summaries give 2,521-2,800); Meir's 1,500-2,000 figure is contemporaneous (FRUS 1969-76 XXV, Document 259). Egyptian and Syrian totals are secondary-literature ranges. The Al Jazeera 2017 article URL is in the older 'indepth/features' format found verbatim in a citation corpus and may redirect.

Oil embargo: FRUS confirms the Kuwait announcement of 17 October 1973 (11 producers, 5 per cent cut), Libya's 19 October and Saudi Arabia's 20 October halts of exports to the United States, and the OAPEC decision in Vienna on 18 March 1974 to lift the embargo; the quadrupling of posted prices is attributed to the Federal Reserve History essay and the US Office of the Historian milestone, which were not opened. Nixon's aid request date (19 October) is the standard date.

Sinai I: the signing at noon on 18 January 1974 at Kilometer 101, witnessed by General Siilasvuo, is confirmed by the announcement text in FRUS 1969-76 XXVI, Documents 8-10; the completion of implementation by early March 1974 is the standard chronology and was not read here. The marker coordinates for Kilometre 101 (about 30.05 N, 32.20 E) are approximate.

Israel-Syria disengagement: FRUS confirms the announcement that the agreement would be signed in Geneva on 31 May 1974 (an earlier draft said 30 May) and the limited-forces terms; Security Council resolution 350 of 31 May 1974 welcomed the agreement and created UNDOF. The June 1974 prisoner exchange and the withdrawal timetable are from the standard chronology.

Refworld URLs are cited in https form; the resolution text files carry them in http form (http://www.refworld.org/docid/...). Refworld has since reorganised its site and these document IDs may redirect.

Cairo Agreement (Lebanon-PLO): FRUS 1969-76 XXIII, Document 60 dates the 'so-called Cairo Agreement' to 2 November 1969, whereas most accounts give 3 November; the event was excluded rather than resolve the discrepancy without a second source.
